analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $17 over six years and ends sub-minimum wages for tipped, teen, and disabled workers.
analysis.headline: The Raise the Wage Act of 2025 has 35 Senate supporters but has not received a single committee action since being referred in April 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would raise the federal minimum wage in steps, from $9.50 an hour starting three months after enactment up to $17 an hour five years later, after which it would rise automatically with median wage growth [S2]. It would also gradually eliminate the lower minimum wage for tipped workers, the lower wage for newly hired teenagers, and the special certificates that let employers pay workers with disabilities below the minimum [S2]. The bill has 34 Democratic cosponsors plus its Independent sponsor, but it was referred to the Senate labor committee and has had no hearings, markup, or vote since [S1] [S3] [S4].
analysis.who_benefits: Roughly the lowest-paid segment of the workforce: workers earning at or near the federal minimum of $7.25 an hour, including tipped restaurant workers currently guaranteed as little as $2.13 in base cash wages, newly hired teens, and workers with disabilities in jobs paying less than the minimum under special certificates. The phased schedule and automatic indexing are designed to raise pay without a sudden shock, and the bill requires the Labor Department to publish notice before each increase [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage from $7.25 to $9.50 on the effective date, then in annual steps to $11.00, $12.50, $14.00, $15.50, and $17.00, with automatic annual increases thereafter tied to growth in the median hourly wage so the floor does not erode again [S2].

Phases out the tipped sub-minimum wage: the base cash wage for tipped employees rises from $6.00 to $17.00 over six years, after which tipped workers get the full minimum wage, and the bill affirmatively guarantees employees the right to keep their tips [S2].
Phases out the sub-minimum wage for newly hired workers under 20 and repeals that exception entirely once the youth wage reaches the regular minimum [S2].

Phases out special certificates allowing employers to pay workers with disabilities below the minimum: their wage floor rises to $5.00, $7.50, $10.00, $12.50, and $15.50 before reaching the full minimum five years later, no new certificates may be issued, and the program sunsets, with Labor Department transition assistance for affected employers and workers [S2].
Requires the Secretary of Labor to publish advance notice of each increase in the Federal Register and on the Department of Labor website [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers who pay at or near the minimum wage, concentrated in restaurants, hotels, retail, agriculture, and disability service providers. Restaurants would face the largest change because the bill eliminates the tipped-employer credit that currently lets them pay as little as $2.13 in base wages where tips cover the difference. Under current law these employers bear the cost directly; economic research cited on both sides of past debates disputes how much falls on prices, profits, or jobs.

drawbacks.text: Employers and their associations have long argued that sharp minimum wage increases raise costs for small businesses and reduce entry-level or part-time hours; the restaurant industry in particular opposes ending the tip credit, which it says would force tipped servers onto wages that do not reflect their actual tip income. These are the standard objections an honest supporter must answer, and the bill's six-year phase-in and indexing are its answer to them [S2].

Ending the section 14(c) sub-minimum program raises a genuine transition concern: employers holding those certificates get technical assistance, but workers in sheltered workshop settings could face job loss if providers cannot or will not pay full minimum wages, which is why the bill directs the Labor Department to help ensure continuing employment opportunities [S2].

The bill sets no regional adjustment, so a $17 floor applies uniformly in low-wage rural areas and high-cost cities alike; supporters see this as equal protection of the floor, critics see it as ignoring local cost differences.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers earning near $7.25 an hour, the bill's benefit is direct and large: a raise of more than double over six years, extended to tipped, teen, and disabled workers who today can legally be paid far less. The costs fall on specific employers, and the strongest objections—pressure on small restaurants and the transition out of sheltered-workshop pay—are real but are partially addressed by the long phase-in, tip-protection language, and transition assistance. The bill is a straightforward transfer of income from employer margins and prices to low-wage workers; its main design risk is the uniform national floor rather than any hidden defect.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee in April 2025, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote has been scheduled since; with the chamber still in session, it sits waiting for committee action that has not come.

narrative.text: Senator Sanders introduced the Raise the Wage Act of 2025 on April 8, 2025, joined by 34 Democratic cosponsors [S1] [S3].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S4].
As of the latest action history, the committee has taken no further action on the bill—no hearing, no markup, no vote—and it has not reached the Senate floor [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: At this stage, employers who pay at or near the minimum wage—especially restaurant chains and hotel operators that rely on the tipped-employee sub-minimum—are better off, because no increase has been enacted and the bill has not moved. Workers covered by the $7.25 federal floor have gained nothing from the bill so far.

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.role: U.S. Senator from Vermont; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Raise the Wage Act of 2025 and gathered cosponsor support.

for.name: 34 Democratic senators
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, including Senators Alsobrooks, Baldwin, Blumenthal, Booker, Duckworth, Durbin, Fetterman, Gillibrand, Klobuchar, Markey, Murray, Sanders allies, Schiff, Warren, Welch, Whitehouse, and Wyden.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral: no hearing, markup, or vote on the bill has been scheduled since April 2025.

sides.party_line_note: All 34 cosponsors are Democrats and the sponsor is an Independent who caucuses with Democrats; no Republican has signed on, and the bill is in a committee controlled by the Republican majority, which has not acted on it [S3] [S4].

industries.note: The bill phases out the tip credit, ending these employers' ability to pay a base cash wage far below the minimum and requiring the full minimum wage plus tips. Their cost savings come directly out of the lowest-paid workers' guaranteed pay, so in this bill their interest runs against those workers' [S2].

industries.industry: Sheltered workshop and disability service providers holding 14(c) certificates
industries.note: The bill raises their legal wage floor and sunsets the certificates that let them pay workers with disabilities below the minimum. Their lower labor costs came at the price of sub-minimum pay to workers, which is what the bill ends [S2].

industries.industry: Other minimum-wage employers (retail, fast food, agriculture, cleaning services)
industries.note: These employers would face steadily rising wage floors over six years, with the option to absorb the cost through prices, automation, or margins. The wage floor they pay below is the income floor for the workers the bill aims to lift [S2].

analysis.trajectory: Bills raising the federal minimum wage have repeatedly been introduced by Senator Sanders and stalled in committee under both parties; with a Republican Senate majority that has not scheduled any action in the roughly half-year since referral, the realistic path is that this bill sits in committee and expires at the end of the 119th Congress without a vote, unless wage politics force it onto the floor through other vehicles.
